Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-08-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (AE - Redwood), Samira (SE - Redwood), Jaya (NovaHealth), Priya (NovaHealth security), Mike (NovaHealth infra), Liam (contractor)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Deep dive on PrivateLink cross-account setup, MTU and TCP MSS issues observed with large batched gRPC/rpc payloads, and recommendations for NAT/egress and DNS split-horizon for control plane/data plane split.
- Action items: network diagram, privatelink test artifacts, benchmark config, follow-up lab.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Samira, our infra SE. How's everyone?
[00:12] Jaya: Hi, thanks. We're excited. We had some flaky behavior with our Private VPC deployment — saw packet fragmentation and intermittent timeouts when we bumped batch sizes for inference.
[00:22] Samira: Okay, thanks. We'll walk through the cross-account PrivateLink setup first, then MTU and the runtime symptoms like KV cache hit rate drops under fragmentation.
[00:34] Mike: Quick note — NovaHealth has a corporate firewall and an outbound proxy that we can't change, so traffic goes via a NAT gateway in our shared-services VPC, then egress through a transit setup.
[00:47] Priya: Also security question up front: control plane must not see PHI, so we need clear data plane routing and mTLS for the data plane. We'll want KMS/HSM note too.
[00:58] Alex: Totally. Our standard private deployment model separates the control plane (Redwood account) from the data plane (customer VPC). For PrivateLink we create an endpoint service in our account and you accept it in yours; cross-account acceptance and policy are key.
[01:14] Samira: Two quick architecture patterns we've seen: 1) Interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) for control-plane RPCs and model pulls; 2) S3/ECR gateway endpoints for large model layer pulls to avoid internet egress. You can combine both.
[01:30] Jaya: We mostly used interface endpoints but still saw MTU issues. Packets show 1500 -> fragment -> retransmit on large payloads.
[01:40] Samira: Right — PrivateLink interfaces create ENIs in your subnets; MTU stays 1500 unless you enable jumbo frames in your VPC (9001) and all hops support it. More often the culprit is MSS clamping not happening and your proxy/NAT device doing TCP segmentation offload incorrectly.
[01:58] Mike: Our NAT is an F5 box before transit, and we suspect it touches MSS.
[02:05] Samira: That matches. For gRPC-heavy workloads, payloads can be large when batching tokens into a single request — if TCP segments are fragmented you see head-of-line blocking and latency spikes, which also causes lower KV cache hit rates because requests time out and clients re-open contexts.
[02:26] Jaya: We're seeing latency go from 40ms to 800ms under heavier batches.
[02:31] Alex: Two knobs to look at: reduce batch size or switch to chunked streaming; and fix network MTU/MSS so packets don't fragment. We prefer to preserve batch size and fix network where possible.
[02:43] Priya: From security, if we change subnets/MTU we need clear change windows but okay. Also, what's the impact of using a NAT gateway versus interface endpoint for model downloads?
[02:57] Samira: If you use NAT for model pulls you egress to S3/ECR over internet which adds unknown paths; better to use S3 gateway endpoints or VPC endpoints for ECR to keep traffic local in the region. NAT increases complexity: source/dest check, ephemeral ports, and makes tracebacks harder.
[03:18] Mike: About the privatelink cross-account acceptance: do we need to open specific principals or can we limit to our account ID?
[03:26] Alex: You can limit to account IDs or roles. The endpoint service owner (Redwood) shares the service name and you create an interface endpoint in your account and accept it. For cross-account, we usually ask customers to set allowedPrincipals to the Redwood service principal or specific account. We'll share a CloudFormation example.
[03:41] Liam: Any special SG rules?
[03:44] Samira: Interface endpoints need permissive SG egress/ingress for the control plane ports — typically HTTPS 443 and a gRPC-multiplexed port (we use 443 with HTTP/2). You'll need SG allowing outbound to the endpoint ENIs and inbound from them for callback flows if you host callbacks.
[03:59] Jaya: DNS — we're using Route53 private hosted zone and split-horizon for internal names. Should we create conditional forwarding or use the VPC resolver?
[04:08] Alex: Good question. Two patterns: 1) We recommend using the VPC resolver and Route53 private hosted zones so privatelink service name resolves to the interface endpoint IPs in your VPC. 2) If you're using split-horizon across accounts, ensure the resolver rules point to the correct inbound endpoints or use conditional forwarders — mis-resolved names can end up going to public endpoints and breaking connectivity.
[04:27] Priya: We also have to ensure DNS logs for audit are captured; will Redwood's control plane produce connection-level logs without data payload?
[04:35] Samira: We emit connection-level metadata (timestamps, tokens requested, model id) but redact input text unless you opt-in for debugging. For compliance we can integrate with your KMS and provide audit logs — we'll add the linkage docs.
[04:48] Alex: Back to MTU: a quick test — run iperf with 1500 and 9000 between a host in your subnet and the privatelink ENI. Also check tcpdump for 'fragmented-ip' flags. If you see fragmentation, MSS clamping on the F5/NAT or your firewall is required, or set tcp_mtu_probing on Linux side.
[05:09] Mike: We'll run iperf and upload pcap.
[05:13] Jaya: What about the control/data plane split causing egress through another account and thus breaking our outbound proxy?
[05:20] Samira: If the control plane egress goes through Redwood-managed infra in our account, you can still route traffic to the interface endpoints and ensure the data stays in your VPC. The key is to avoid hairpinning via NAT — ensure route tables send traffic to the ENI IPs and not to the NAT gateway.
[05:36] Alex: Also watch for source/destination checks on the ENIs — they must be enabled for interface endpoints. If customers create NAT-based hairpin, flows traverse your NAT and add latency.
[05:46] Jaya: On the runtime side, Samira, you mentioned KV cache hit rate drops. Can you explain how network issues impact caching?
[05:53] Samira: Sure — KV cache lives in GPU memory, but session continuity matters. If clients see transient network errors they restart sessions or reinitialize contexts, which means KV caches are cold. Also, long tail latency causes token timeouts and the client may fallback to smaller batches leading to lower throughput. So network stability equals better effective cache hit and throughput.
[06:14] Alex: For benchmarking we'll want a controlled environment: dedicated pool, fixed batch profile, quantized weights (4-bit or int8), and no proxy. We'll provide a spreadsheet for configs and expected latencies.
[06:25] Samira: For quantization: int8 often reduces memory but can change CPU/GPU kernel choices — that sometimes changes network patterns (smaller payloads vs more frequent calls) so we include both in the benchmark.
[06:37] Priya: Any special ports for metrics/tracing to expose to our observability stack?
[06:43] Alex: We emit metrics to Prometheus endpoints inside the data plane that you can scrape, or we can stream to your CloudWatch/Datadog via a forwarder. Scraping requires SGs and IP whitelisting for the scraper.
[06:55] Mike: For PrivateLink cross-account, do we need to create interface endpoints in each AZ?
[07:01] Samira: Best practice: create interface endpoints in each AZ/subnet where your worker instances live to avoid cross-AZ cross-ENI hops. That reduces latency and avoids cross-AZ data charges.
[07:13] Jaya: We're in three AZs, so we'll add endpoints to all three subnets. Any quota bumps needed?
[07:18] Alex: Yes, interface endpoint ENIs count against EC2 ENI limits and AWS endpoint quotas. We'll include recommended quota numbers in the doc.
[07:26] Liam: A question on certs — do we do TLS termination at the privatelink or at Redwood's service?
[07:31] Samira: TLS is end-to-end; PrivateLink is L3/L2 attach, we still do mutual TLS between your data plane agent and our service. The endpoint is just a tunnel to the service; mTLS ensures only authorized agents talk to the control plane.
[07:44] Priya: For KMS, if we want customer-managed keys, is that supported?
[07:49] Alex: Yes, we can integrate with customer KMS for at-rest encryption on artifacts we store for dedupe/cache keys. We'll need a KMS key policy that allows Redwood's service role to use the key — we'll share sample policies.
[08:02] Mike: About ECR/s3: to avoid expensive egress, should we stage model artifacts in our account?
[08:07] Samira: If you push model layers to your account's S3 and enable gateway endpoints, the data path avoids NAT. Many customers do this for large models. If you can't, we provide presigned pulls over PrivateLink but it's more operationally complex.
[08:22] Jaya: We're also curious about troubleshooting steps if we see fragment/retransmit: what logs to capture?
[08:28] Samira: Capture tcpdump on the host with -s0, sample on the privatelink ENI, and do traceroute -n with TCP mode to port 443. Collect tcpdump, iperf, and kernel dmesg for TCP offload errors. We'll correlate with our side logs.
[08:42] Alex: We'll also run a controlled load test from our dedicated pool to your privatelink IPs to check for per-AZ asymmetry.
[08:50] Mike: Anything about MSS and MTU best practice?
[08:53] Samira: Keep MTU 1500 unless you can guarantee jumbo frames end-to-end. If you can't, enable MSS clamping on the NAT/firewall to 1400-ish or set tcp_mtu_probing=1 on Linux to handle path MTU discovery.
[09:07] Jaya: Understood. On the Redwood runtime: does batching happen client-side or server-side?
[09:12] Samira: Both patterns exist. Client-side batching aggregates multiple app requests into a single inference call. Server-side continuous batching accumulates in the runtime for a small window. For low-latency apps we rely more on server-side and small client-side batches; for throughput we push batching to the client. Network fragmentation impacts both.
[09:28] Alex: Also, intelligent KV cache prefix caching reduces repeat token transmission; but if the session resets network-wise you lose that state so caching benefits drop.
[09:36] Priya: For canarying changes, what's a safe rollout strategy?
[09:40] Alex: Start with canary in a single AZ, small percent of traffic, monitor latency, KV cache hit, and error rates. If metrics look good, expand. We support per-route rollout policies in the Console.
[09:53] Jaya: Any gotchas with Security groups when using multiple endpoints across AZs?
[09:58] Samira: Ensure SGs allow the private endpoint ENI CIDR range and your worker IP ranges; avoid overly broad egress rules, but also avoid blocking ephemeral ports needed for TLS handshake.
[10:10] Liam: We saw a note in a forum about TCP window scaling and long RTT affecting throughput — relevant?
[10:15] Samira: Yes, if RTTs increase due to transit hops you need TCP window tuning for high throughput. For inference tokenization, keep RTTs small and windows default are usually fine; if you do cross-region, tune accordingly.
[10:27] Alex: Quick recap and final items — we'll send the privatelink checklist, the CFN sample, and the benchmark spreadsheet. Customer will run iperf/traceroute and share pcaps, then we'll schedule the lab session.
[10:39] Jaya: Sounds good. Anything else from you?
[10:42] Priya: Please include the KMS policy sample and the list of logs we can expect without sharing PII.
[10:49] Samira: Yep we'll include those.
[10:51] Alex: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed lab time.
[10:56] Mike: Thanks.
[11:00] (call ends)
